record.context_brief: Physical basis and redshift evolution of Type Ia standardization
record.original_question: Why does the empirical Type Ia supernova standardization relation work—brighter Type Ia supernovae evolve photometrically more slowly than fainter ones—and how much cosmological bias can arise if the high-redshift population has a different balance of fast progenitors with lifetimes under about 100 million years and tardy progenitors that typically explode more than 1 billion years after formation?

evidence.quote: Even if SNIa are commonly referred to as ideal standard candles because of their high luminosity at explosion and their relatively narrow range of observational properties, they are not quite perfect and, maybe, not even standard.
Standardization is obtained exploiting the empirical evidence that bright SNIa evolve photometrically more slowly than faint SNIa.

However, even if this phenomenon is measured rather accurately in the local Universe so as to lead to accurate empirical corrections, its physical nature is far from understood and, therefore, this standardization rests on unsecure grounds.

Moreover, when moving to higher redshifts [7] , i.e. to the past phases of the evolution of the Universe, the balance between fast evolving SNIa progenitors (with lifetimes less than about 100 Myrs) and the “tardy" ones (that typically explode more than 1 Gyr after formation) shifts in favor of the fast component, so that any systematic difference between the two components will bias the observational results.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are used as cosmological distance indicators by exploiting an empirical luminosity–light-curve relation: intrinsically brighter SNe Ia decline photometrically more slowly than fainter ones, and after correction with this relation their peak magnitudes are nearly standard. Two channels of progenitor systems are believed to contribute to the observed SN Ia rate: a "prompt" or fast-evolving channel whose progenitors explode less than about 100 Myr after star formation, and a "tardy" or delayed channel whose progenitors explode more than about 1 Gyr after star formation. The relative fraction of these two channels varies with cosmic time, so that high-redshift samples are dominated by the prompt component while low-redshift samples have a larger tardy contribution.

(a) Provide a physical explanation, derived from the explosion mechanism and progenitor properties, of why the empirical brighter-slower / fainter-faster relation holds and identify the underlying parameter (e.g. progenitor mass, metallicity, central density, or 56Ni yield) responsible for the simultaneous variation of peak luminosity and light-curve decline rate.

(b) Assuming that the prompt and tardy populations have systematically different mean standardized absolute magnitudes ΔM (after applying the standard brighter-slower correction), and letting f_prompt(z) denote the prompt fraction as a function of redshift z, quantify the resulting bias in the inferred distance modulus μ(z) and the consequent bias on cosmological parameters (in particular on the dark-energy equation-of-state parameters w_0 and w_a) as a function of z and ΔM. Determine how large ΔM must be in order to produce a bias in w_0 or w_a that exceeds current observational uncertainties.
artifact.status_search_result: The physical origin of the brighter-slower relation is still not fully understood, but recent work has accumulated strong evidence that progenitor age (linked to the prompt vs. tardy channel balance) is a dominant driver of post-standardization luminosity differences and induces a redshift-dependent systematic bias in SN Ia cosmology. Studies in 2020–2025 quantify this bias and argue that it is largely uncorrected by the conventional host-mass step and may significantly affect inferred dark-energy parameters, but a complete first-principles physical theory and a definitive correction scheme remain unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Type Ia supernova progenitors: a contemporary view of a long-standing puzzle
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews the unresolved progenitor problem of SNe Ia, including the prompt/tardy (delay-time) framework.
status_evidence.claim: The physical nature of SN Ia progenitors and the standardization relation remains an open puzzle.

status_evidence.title: Strong progenitor age bias in supernova cosmology – I
status_evidence.snippet: Significant correlation between standardized SN magnitude and progenitor age introduces a serious redshift-dependent systematic bias in SN cosmology, largely uncorrected by the mass step.
status_evidence.claim: Progenitor-age-driven cosmological bias has been quantified and shown to be significant.

status_evidence.title: Strong progenitor age bias in supernova cosmology – II
status_evidence.snippet: Argues alignment with DESI BAO once age bias is corrected, with implications for dark-energy parameters.
status_evidence.claim: Recent studies estimate the magnitude of the cosmological bias from prompt/tardy progenitor mix.

status_evidence.title: Redshift evolution of the underlying type Ia supernova stretch distribution
status_evidence.snippet: Two populations of SNe Ia: one from young (<100 Myr) and one from older (Gyr) progenitors; the underlying stretch distribution evolves with redshift.
status_evidence.claim: The prompt/tardy split with the stated lifetime thresholds is empirically supported and evolves with z.
